In the Byzantine New Testament it appears only 3 times, rendered "servant" twice (as when Mary calls herself the Lord's servant) and once alongside menservants. It's far more common in the Septuagint, where it appears 39 times and most often translates the Hebrew words אָמָה (21×) and שִׁפְחָה (15×), both terms for a maidservant or bondwoman.
prose.caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences this word's range rests largely on Septuagint evidence.

prose.def: A person owned as a slave or bound servant, lower in status than free people and masters.
prose.article: δοῦλον is a form of the noun δοῦλος, meaning a slave or servant—someone owned as property or otherwise bound to serve another. Abbott-Smith notes the word can also be used figuratively, in a bad sense for moral or spiritual bondage and in a good sense for a devoted minister, though those usages come from the wider δοῦλος evidence rather than this specific form. This particular form is very rare in the surveyed corpus, appearing 0 times in the Byzantine New Testament and only once in the Septuagint.
prose.caution: Evidence for this exact form is extremely thin—no Byzantine NT occurrences and just one Septuagint use—so its meaning is inferred from the parent word δοῦλος.
